### Question 1

- *mutually exclusive events* are events that cannot occur simultaneously, meaning they are dependent - or the state of one event effects the state of the other
-  *independent events* are events that do not influence each other in any way, or the state of one event does not impact the state of the other

### Question 2
> I use the following terminology because I've worked with Bayesian networks in my research work. I love Bayesian!
- Traditional probabilistic operations "feed forward," or allow you to predict *effect* from *cause*.
- *Bayes Theorem* let's you **reverse the conditional** or calculate *cause from effect
- In diagnostic testing, you can use *priors*, or the prior known knowledge of *prevalence, sensitivity, and specificity* to calculate positive and negative predictive value(s) in non-representative samples. 

## Question 3
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(G)      &= 0.141 &&\text{where } G = \{\text{gestational age }<37\ \text{weeks}\},\\
P(W)      &= 0.047 &&\text{where } W = \{\text{birth weight }<2500\ \text{g}\},\\
P(G \cap W) &= 0.029 &&\text{(both events occur).}
\end{aligned}
$$
**A**: ![[Pasted image 20250914085724.png]]
> Made using Python and Matplotlib

**B**:Two events are independent if $P(A|B) = P(A)$.
	- $P(A|B) = \cfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} = \cfrac{0.029}{0.047} = 0.617 \ne P(A)$ 
	- these two events are **dependent**
**C**: Probability of A or B or Both occuring is 
$$P(A)+P(B)-(A \cap B) = 0.141+0.047-0.029 = 0.159 \\
\\\\\ \text{ OR }
\\
1-0.841 = 0.159
$$
	- **0.159**
**D**: $P(A|B) = \cfrac{P(A\bigcap B)}{P(B)} = \cfrac{0.029}{0.047} = 0.617$

## Question 4
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Sensitivity }(Se) &= P(\text{Test} + \mid \text{Disease}) = 0.72,\\
\text{Specificity }(Sp) &= P(\text{Test} - \mid \text{No Disease}) = 0.60.
\end{aligned}
$$
**A**: 
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{PPV} &= P(D \mid T^{+})
   = \frac{Se \times Prev}{Se \times Prev + (1 - Sp) \times (1 - Prev)}, \\[6pt]
\text{NPV} &= P(D^{c} \mid T^{-})
   = \frac{Sp \times (1 - Prev)}{Sp \times (1 - Prev) + (1 - Se) \times Prev}.
\end{aligned}
$$

 $$
\begin{aligned}
\text{For } Prev = 0.17:& 
\\
\text{PPV} &= \frac{Se \times 0.17}{Se \times 0.17 + (1 - Sp) \times (1 - 0.17)}, \\
\text{NPV} &= \frac{Sp \times (1 - 0.17)}{Sp \times (1 - 0.17) + (1 - Se) \times 0.17}; \\[10pt]
\\
\text{PPV} = 0.270
\\
\text{NPV} = 0.913
\end{aligned}
$$
**B**:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{For } Prev = 0.12:& \\
\text{PPV} &= \frac{Se \times 0.12}{Se \times 0.12 + (1 - Sp) \times (1 - 0.12)}, \\
\text{NPV} &= \frac{Sp \times (1 - 0.12)}{Sp \times (1 - 0.12) + (1 - Se) \times 0.12}; \\[10pt]
\\
\text{PPV} = 0.197
\\
\text{NPV} = 0.940
\\
\\
\\
\text{For } Prev = 0.07:& \\
\text{PPV} &= \frac{Se \times 0.07}{Se \times 0.07 + (1 - Sp) \times (1 - 0.07)}, \\
\text{NPV} &= \frac{Sp \times (1 - 0.07)}{Sp \times (1 - 0.07) + (1 - Se) \times 0.07};
\\
\text{PPV} = 0.119
\\
\text{NPV} = 0.966
\end{aligned}
$$

## Question 5

| Method    | Probability of Pregnancy |
| --------- | ------------------------ |
| None      | 0.430                    |
| Diaphragm | 0.152                    |
| Condom    | 0.099                    |
| IUD       | 0.065                    |
| Phil      | 0.036                    |
$$
\begin{flalign*}
& X   = \text{Pregnant} &\\
& X^C = \text{Not Pregnant} &\\
& M   = \text{Method of Contraception} &\\
& M^C = \text{No Contraception Used} &\\[30pt]

& RR  = \cfrac{P(X|M)}{P(X|M^C)} &
\end{flalign*}
$$

*After plugging in $P(X|M)$ and $P(X|M^C)$ for each method we get the following*

| METHOD    | RELATIVE RISK (RR) |
| --------- | ------------------ |
| Diaphragm | 0.353              |
| Condom    | 0.230              |
| IUD       | 0.151              |
| Phil      | 0.083              |


## Question 6

- $A \cap B$ is the *intersection* between $A$ and $B$ or the probability of both $A$ **AND** $B$ occurring simultaneously  
- $A \cup B$ is the *union* between $A$ and $B$ or the probability of either $A$ **OR** $B$ occuring
- $A^C$ is the event that the individual **is not** pregnant
- **No**. They are not mutually exclusive. They would only be if they could not occur simultaneously, which is not the case.

## Question 7

**A.**  
$$
P(X \le 29)
= 0.001 + 0.082 + 0.228 + 0.301
= \mathbf{0.612}
$$

**B.**  
$$
P(X \ge 35)
= 0.110 + 0.031 + 0.002
= \mathbf{0.143}
$$

**C.**  
$$
P(X > 19 \mid X < 30)
= \frac{0.228 + 0.301}{0.001 + 0.082 + 0.228 + 0.301}
= \frac{0.529}{0.612}
\approx \mathbf{0.864}
$$

**D.**  
$$
P(X < 40 \mid X \ge 30)
= \frac{0.245 + 0.110}{0.245 + 0.110 + 0.031 + 0.002}
= \frac{0.355}{0.388}
\approx \mathbf{0.914}
$$

## Question 8

**A.** $$
\begin{aligned}
\cfrac{95}{1,612,253} = 0.0000589 \\
\\
\text{Or as a proportion of 100,000} \\
\\
100,000*(\cfrac{95}{1,612,253}) = 5.89 \quad \text{per 100,000}
\end{aligned}
$$

**B.** $$
\begin{aligned}

\cfrac{444}{918,756} = 0.000483 \\
\\
\text{Or as a proportion of 100,000} \\
\\
100,000*\cfrac{444}{918,756} = 48.3 \quad \text{per 100,000}
\end{aligned}
$$
**C.** $$
\begin{aligned}
RR  = \cfrac{P(X|M)}{P(X|M^C)}\\
\begin{flalign*}\\\\
& \text{Where} &\\
& X = \text{Hospitalized} &\\
& X^C = \text{Not Hospitalized} &\\
& M = \text{Vaccinated} &\\
& M^C = \text{Not Vaccinated}
\end{flalign*} \\\\
RR = \cfrac{(95/1,612,253)}{(444/918,756)} = \cfrac{0.0000589}{0.000483} = 0.12 \\
\end{aligned}
$$
*Vaccinated adults had **12%** of the risk of hospitalization compared with unvaccinated adults*


## Question 9

The probability of someone in this age group having covid $P(C) = \cfrac{3275}{503567} = 0.00650$

Let $X$ be the number of positive test results

The probability of at least one person in 100 having covid $P(X \ge 1)$ can be rewritten as $1-P(X=0)$ 

This can be solved by computing:
$$
`\begin{aligned}
P(X=k)=\dbinom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}
\\\\
\text{which can be simplified because k = 0} 
\\\\
\dbinom{n}{0}p^0(1-p)^n
\\
=(1-p)^n
\\
=(1-0.00650)^{100}
\\
= 0.520 
\\\\
\text{don't forget to subtract from 1}
\\
1 - 0.520 = 0.479
\end{aligned}`
$$

## Question 10

**A.**  
For the 29-year-old ($p_1 = 0.249$) and the 36-year-old ($p_2 = 0.249$), the probability that **both are uninsured** is  
$$
P(\text{both uninsured}) = p_1 \times p_2
= 0.249 \times 0.249
\approx 0.0620
$$

**B.**  
The probability that **both have insurance** is  
$$
P(\text{both insured}) = (1 - p_1) \times (1 - p_2)
= (1 - 0.249) \times (1 - 0.249)
= 0.751 \times 0.751
\approx 0.564
$$

**C.**  
For the 53-year-old ($p_3 = 0.163$) and the 19-year-old ($p_4 = 0.249$), the probability that **both are uninsured** is  
$$
P(\text{both uninsured}) = p_3 \times p_4
= 0.163 \times 0.249
\approx 0.0406
$$

**D.**  
The probability that **both have insurance** is  
$$
P(\text{both insured}) = (1 - p_3) \times (1 - p_4)
= (1 - 0.163) \times (1 - 0.249)
= 0.837 \times 0.751
\approx 0.628
$$

## Question 11

**A.**  
The probability of a **false negative** is the probability that the test is negative given the disease is present.  
If sensitivity is $0.379$, then  
$$
P(\text{False Negative})
= 1 - \text{Sensitivity}
= 1 - 0.379
= 0.621
$$

**B.**  
The probability of a **false positive** is the probability that the test is positive given no disease.  
If specificity is $0.631$, then  
$$
P(\text{False Positive})
= 1 - \text{Specificity}
= 1 - 0.631
= 0.369
$$

**C.**  
Let prevalence be $P(D) = 0.029$.  
Using Bayes’ theorem, the probability of cancer given a positive test is  
$$
P(D \mid +)
= \frac{\text{Sensitivity} \times P(D)}
{\text{Sensitivity} \times P(D) + (1 - \text{Specificity}) \times [1 - P(D)]}
$$
Plugging in the values,
$$
P(D \mid +)
= \frac{0.379 \times 0.029}
{0.379 \times 0.029 + 0.369 \times 0.971}
\approx \frac{0.0110}{0.0110 + 0.358}
\approx \frac{0.0110}{0.369}
\approx 0.0298
$$
So the probability is about **0.0298** (≈ **2.98%**).


## Question 12
**A.**  
Sensitivity is the probability the dipstick test is positive **given** the culture test is positive.  
$$
\text{Sensitivity}
= \frac{90}{99}
\approx 0.909
$$  
Specificity is the probability the dipstick test is negative **given** the culture test is negative.  
$$
\text{Specificity}
= \frac{86}{125}
\approx 0.688
$$

**B.**  
Given a population prevalence $P(D)=0.11$, and using sensitivity $0.909$ and specificity $0.688$,  
$$
P(D \mid +)
= \frac{0.909 \times 0.11}
{0.909 \times 0.11 + (1 - 0.688) \times (1 - 0.11)}
$$
Compute:
$$
0.909 \times 0.11 = 0.100 \\
1 - 0.688 = 0.312,\quad 1 - 0.11 = 0.89 \\
0.312 \times 0.89 \approx 0.278 \\
P(D \mid +) \approx \frac{0.100}{0.100 + 0.278}
\approx 0.265
$$

**C.**  
Predictive value of a negative test is  
$$
P(D^c \mid -)
= \frac{0.688 \times 0.89}
{0.688 \times 0.89 + (1 - 0.909) \times 0.11}
$$
Compute:
$$
0.688 \times 0.89 \approx 0.613 \\
1 - 0.909 = 0.091 \\
0.091 \times 0.11 \approx 0.0100 \\
P(D^c \mid -) \approx \frac{0.613}{0.613 + 0.0100}
\approx 0.984
$$


## Question 13

**A.**  
Probability of CHD in each class:
$$
P(\text{CHD|I}) = \frac{107}{599} \approx 0.179 \\
P(\text{CHD|III}) = \frac{644}{3063} \approx 0.210 \\
P(\text{CHD|V}) = \frac{99}{422} \approx 0.235
$$

**B.**  
Odds of CHD in each class:
$$
\text{Odds}_{III} = \frac{644}{2419} \approx 0.266 \\
\text{Odds}_{V} = \frac{99}{323} \approx 0.306 \\
\text{Odds}_{I} = \frac{107}{492} \approx 0.217
$$
Relative to class I:
$$
\text{OR}_{III/I} = \frac{0.266}{0.217} \approx 1.23 \\
\text{OR}_{V/I} = \frac{0.306}{0.217} \approx 1.41
$$

**C.**  
Because the probabilities and odds of CHD rise from social class I to III to V,  
there is evidence of a positive association between **lower social class** and **higher CHD risk**.
